abstract: Insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes occur in Bardet-Biedl syndrome, and BBSome proteins regulate insulin receptor abundance at the cell surface in mammals. We asked how loss of two structurally related BBSome subunits, BBS1 and BBS9, affects development on a high-sucrose diet in Drosophila melanogaster. Sequence comparisons identified the seven-bladed beta-propeller and gamme-adaptin ear domains of human BBS1 and BBS9 in their respective fly orthologues. High sucrose (1 M) delayed pupariation in both single mutants, with the longest delay in flies lacking both subunits. The double mutant already showed a delay on standard sucrose (0.15 M). On high sucrose, its first pupae were recorded at 216 h after egg laying, whereas the last control and single-mutant pupae had formed by 168 h. Loss of BBS1 also reduced pupal volume and adult wing area on high sucrose. Both measurements remained close to control values in BBS9 mutants. These findings suggest overlapping contributions of BBS1 and BBS9 to developmental timing and a greater requirement for BBS1 to sustain growth under high dietary sucrose.
